opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the frontier is never where you expect it to be, so you have to keep probing for it rather than assuming you know.

A lot of people measure progress with benchmarks, and benchmarks are useful, but they saturate quickly, and once a system gets very good at a benchmark you start asking whether it's actually reasoning or just very well-adapted to that distribution of problems. So for us, a big part of finding the real frontier is constantly building new problems we haven't seen, ones that are slightly out of reach. If the system solves everything you give it, you've learned very little. If it fails at everything, you've also learned very little. The interesting zone is right at the edge, where it succeeds maybe some of the time and you can study why it succeeds or fails.

The second thing is that in math we have something most fields don't: verification. When you work in a formal setting, a proof either checks or it doesn't. That makes the frontier much more measurable. You're not arguing over whether an answer "looks right." You can see exactly which step broke, whether the model got lost in the search, whether it lacked a lemma, or whether it never had the right idea in the first place. Those are very different failure modes, and they point to very different things you need to build.

Third, I spend a lot of time talking with working mathematicians, because their intuition about what is hard is often different from what is hard for a machine. Some things that take a human years to learn, like heavy computation or keeping track of many cases, can be easy for a system. And some things a first-year grad student finds obvious, like choosing the right abstraction or noticing that two problems are secretly the same, turn out to be really difficult. The real frontier lives in that mismatch, so you have to take both perspectives seriously.

Finally, I try to keep the team honest about the difference between a demo and a capability. One beautiful solved problem is exciting, but the question I keep asking is: can we do this reliably, across a whole family of problems, without us quietly steering it? If the answer is no, then that isn't the frontier yet. It's a glimpse of where the frontier might be heading, and that's where the work starts.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd say is that benchmarks don't tell you where the frontier is. They tell you where the frontier was when somebody wrote the benchmark. By the time a problem set is public, it's been studied, it's been discussed, there are solutions floating around online, and so a high score often means the model has absorbed the surroundings of the problem rather than that it can actually do the mathematics.

So the way we think about it is a bit different. We try to find problems that nobody has solved yet. Not contrived problems, but real ones, the kind that sit in a working mathematician's notebook. Those are the only problems where you really can't fake it. There's no answer key to leak. Either the argument holds up under scrutiny or it doesn't.

Practically, that means we spend a lot of time talking to mathematicians. People in number theory, combinatorics, analysis, who have questions they've been stuck on, or lemmas they believe but haven't proved, or cases they haven't checked. We ask them for problems that are hard for a reason, not hard because they're obscure. And then we see what happens when the system takes them on.

What's interesting is that failure is actually the most informative part. When the model gets something wrong, we look very carefully at how it got it wrong. Did it make a plausible-looking leap that doesn't hold? Did it misunderstand the object? Did it get lost in the bookkeeping? Each of those is a different kind of weakness, and each tells us something different about what to build next.

And the frontier moves. Something that was impossible six months ago becomes routine, and then you have to go find the next thing that's impossible. So I'd say the approach is really a discipline of staying uncomfortable. If we're mostly succeeding, we're probably asking the wrong questions. The right place to be is where we're failing maybe more often than we're winning, but the wins are real, and they're verified by people who would know.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between a problem the team can solve reliably and a problem where everything has to go right. Those tell you different things about your capabilities.

So I would look closely at where we get stuck. Can we find the right representation? Can we identify a useful intermediate claim? Once we have an idea, can we actually turn it into a rigorous proof? A final answer alone doesn’t tell you which of those abilities is missing.

And then I’d vary the problem a little. If a small change breaks the approach, that’s useful information: perhaps we understood a particular example, but not the underlying structure. If the approach keeps working across variations, I’d feel more confident pushing further.

To me, the frontier is where we can still make meaningful progress, but we can’t yet explain how to make that progress consistently. That’s where I’d want the team spending time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between a problem the team hasn’t solved yet and a problem that requires an idea the team doesn’t yet know how to find. Those can look very similar from the outside.

So I’d look closely at where progress stops. Can we formulate the problem precisely? Can we solve simpler cases? Do we have a plausible approach but can’t make one step rigorous, or are we missing an approach altogether? Each of those suggests a different limitation.

And then I’d vary the problem or give a small hint. If one hint unlocks the whole solution, that tells you something quite different from a case where every step requires help. The interesting frontier is where we can make meaningful progress independently, but we’re still missing something essential. That’s where I’d want to spend time, because it gives us both a challenge and a way to understand what we need to learn.
